title: Building Culture: How to Shape Character Through Daily Interactions https://bunsenblue.com/2024/08/20/building-culture-how-to-shape-character-through-daily-interactions/
author: Pritesh Raichura
summary: Raichura argues that building classroom culture means actively teaching and reinforcing shared values through every daily interaction—not just issuing rules or relying on assemblies about abstract ideals. Values must be made concrete: 'integrity' becomes 'do you pick up the litter even when no one is watching?' The story of Miles catching a dropped tissue and initially ignoring it illustrates how culture-building requires moving from theory to practice in every single moment. Praising students publicly and tying good behavior to a shared identity creates the belonging that motivates lasting change. Raichura explicitly rejects utilitarian rationale ('work hard so you get a good job') in favor of virtue-based reasoning: live these values because it makes you a better person right now. The piece distinguishes between 'managing behaviour' (compliance with rules) and 'building culture' (inspiring students to become better versions of themselves), arguing that the latter requires behaviour management as a foundation but goes significantly further.
points: Values are abstract until made concrete through specific, observable behaviors—'integrity' becomes meaningful when pupils are asked whether they did the right thing when no one was watching, not when it's explained in a general assembly.

Moving from theory to practice in every interaction is the hardest part: it requires teachers to invest time and effort in helping pupils live values not just understand them, in every single moment of the school day.

Appealing to identity and belonging is one of the most powerful levers for behavioural change—when being part of the class means living shared values, pupils gain a way to belong by doing the right thing.
Utilitarian rationale ('work hard to get a good job') is explicitly rejected in favour of virtue ethics: the goal is to become better people right here, right now, not to secure future outcomes.

Building culture is not the same as managing behaviour—behaviour management is a necessary foundation, but building culture means going further to inspire pupils to become better versions of themselves each day.
quotes: I want the pupils in my classroom to become better people each day. This happens when they actually behave in a way that reflects the values we share: integrity, taking responsibility for our actions, thinking about our duty to others, working hard, being grateful, radiating positivity.

To actually invest the time and effort in helping pupils to live those values in every interaction is the tough part. But that is the very thing that will transform culture and forge character in our pupils.

If you can forge an identity where living the values you share is something worth celebrating and worthy of admiration, and explain that being in this class or school means showing integrity, then you allow others in the group a chance to belong
I so often hear teachers narrating behaviours they like to see in utilitarian ways: if you work hard, you will be able to get great qualifications and get the job you want.
I think the phrase 'manage behaviour' sets us up to view our jobs with the paradigm of getting pupils to comply with rules.
If we can make it clear to pupils what those precise actions are and reinforce them continually, through every interaction we have with them, then we can start to build a culture of excellence.
